citation: Montag Jessica L., Jones Michael N., Smith Linda B. (2015). The words children hear: Picture books and the statistics for language learning. Psychological Science. https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797615594361
title: Corpus of 100 children's picture books (68,103 words)
description: A purpose-built corpus of the text of children's picture books that a caregiver might read to infants and very young language learners. The article states: "Our corpus consists of the text of 100 children’s picture books (68,103 words) that a caregiver might read to infants and very young language learners." Titles were selected from librarian-recommended lists, amazon.com bestsellers, and circulation statistics from the Infant and Preschool sections of a public library, targeting books for children 0 to 60 months. The full book list is printed in Table 1.
requirements: No existing corpus of children's picture books existed, so the corpus had to be constructed for the analyses.
constraints: The book sample is relatively small, which the article says underestimates the individual-book diversity pattern.
target_learners: infants and children aged 0 to 60 months
target_learning_goals: early vocabulary learning from child-directed linguistic input
examples: The corpus was compared with 4,432 contiguous CHILDES conversation segments length-matched to the 100 books.
key_sources: Montag Jessica L., Jones Michael N., Smith Linda B. (2015). The words children hear: Picture books and the statistics for language learning. Psychological Science. https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797615594361

article_title: The range of information in Biology: III. Botany.
citation: Grier, N. M. (1918). The Range of Information in Biology. III. Botany. Journal of Educational Psychology, 9, 509-516. https://psycnet.apa.org
title: 100-word range of information test in botany
description: A vocabulary-based diagnostic instrument consisting of 100 botanical terms drawn from grade-school spellers and readers and from Boy Scout and Camp Fire Girls publications, chosen as frequently occurring words. Words were selected to indicate the range of information about plant life pupils might know from nature study and school gardens, and familiarity with biological principles. Pupils were told the terms pertained directly or indirectly to plants.
requirements: Words must be drawn from materials the pupils actually used in grade school work and out-of-school publications
constraints: The method of giving the test is only referenced to previous papers in the series; only the word list is given here
target_learners: first-year high school pupils entering or completing botany
target_learning_goals: range of botanical vocabulary and concepts carried from nature study into secondary biology
examples: The word list printed in the article includes terms such as absorption, anther, carbohydrate, cell, germinate, pollen, and stigma
key_sources: Grier, N. M. (1918). The Range of Information in Biology. III. Botany. Journal of Educational Psychology, 9, 509-516. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0073567
